title: West Nile Virus Hits 22-Year High in the US as Oregon Reports First 2026 Case
excerpt: The CDC has confirmed cases across 23 states, with Arizona accounting for the most infections and four deaths — nearly five times the historical average for this point in the season.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • CDC confirmed 48 West Nile virus cases in 23 states, nearly five times the historical average.
  • Arizona leads with 35 cases and four deaths, marking a severe outbreak.
  • 38 cases are neuroinvasive, indicating the most aggressive start since 2004.
  • Oregon reports its first case of the 2026 season, adding to the growing list.
  • CDC recommends precautions like using DEET and avoiding outdoor activities at dusk.

  • As of late June, the CDC confirmed at least 48 West Nile virus cases across 23 states — nearly five times the historical average of about 10 cases by the end of June.
  • Four deaths have been reported in Arizona, which leads the nation with 35 cases. Oregon has reported its first case of the 2026 season.
  • Of the confirmed cases, 38 are neuroinvasive — the severe form affecting the brain or spinal cord — making this the most aggressive start to a West Nile season since 2004.
  • The CDC recommends using insect repellent containing DEET, wearing long clothing and avoiding outdoor activity at dusk and dawn.

Fastest Start in Two Decades

Federal health officials are warning that the 2026 West Nile virus season has arrived earlier and more aggressively than at any point in the past 22 years. As of June 30, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed at least 48 cases across 23 states, with the numbers climbing rapidly through July.

The pace is alarming. The historical average for West Nile cases by the end of June is roughly 10. This year's count is nearly five times that baseline, with 38 of the confirmed cases classified as neuroinvasive disease — the severe form in which the virus penetrates the brain or spinal cord.

Four deaths have already been reported, all in Arizona, which leads the national count with 35 cases. Single cases have appeared in California, Utah, Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, Nebraska, South Dakota, Illinois and Pennsylvania. Colorado, Oklahoma and Tennessee have each reported two cases.

Oregon's First Case

Oregon has now reported its first West Nile virus case of the 2026 season, adding another state to the growing list. Health officials are advising residents to take precautions, particularly during dusk and dawn hours when mosquitoes that carry the virus are most active.

The state has a documented history with West Nile: in 2006, 73 people were infected in Oregon, one person died, and over 1,000 mosquitoes tested positive. The virus is considered established throughout the contiguous 48 states.

"These findings serve as an important reminder that mosquito season is well underway. As families gather outdoors, we encourage everyone to take simple steps to protect themselves."

— Dr. Erin Staples, CDC Medical Epidemiologist

What You Need to Know

Most people infected with West Nile virus never develop symptoms — roughly 80% of infections are asymptomatic. About one in five infected people experience fever, headache, body aches, joint pain, rash, vomiting or diarrhea. In fewer than 1% of all infections, the virus crosses into the nervous system, causing potentially permanent neurological damage.

People over 50 and those with compromised immune systems face the highest risk of severe illness. There is no vaccine for humans, though one exists for horses.

How to Protect Yourself

The CDC advises several straightforward precautions. Use insect repellent containing DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus or IR-3535. Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants when outdoors, especially between dusk and dawn. Use window screens and air conditioning to keep mosquitoes out of homes. Eliminate standing water around your property — old tires, buckets, birdbaths and pet dishes — where mosquitoes breed.

For Indian families enjoying outdoor summer activities across the US — from backyard barbecues to weekend temple visits — these precautions are particularly relevant in warm-climate states like Arizona, Texas and California, where both mosquito populations and NRI communities are concentrated.
